title: Enlightening wellbeing in the home: The impact of natural light design on perceived happiness and sadness in residential spaces.
research_question: This article studies the relationship between natural lighting in the home and the emotional subjective wellbeing (E-SWB) of its inhabitants, determining which aspects of housing daylight design are more relevant for this.

participants.description: 750 participants from Chile (75.47% from Santiago Metropolitan Region, 68.09% female, 59.05% <30 years old, 52.23% medium income), with a disproportionate number of young adults.
participants.recruitment: Online platform Urban Experiment (www.urban-experiment.com) distributed via social networks, with participants responding using mobile phone, tablet or computer.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: 25 randomly assigned 3D computer simulations of interior housing living spaces (bedroom, kitchen, bathroom, living-dining room) under control (no intervention) and treatment (with daylight design improvements) conditions. Natural lighting conditions were simulated using Sketchup + Vray, based on Santiago, Chile, in winter (June 20th) at 12:00. NLD factors included: distance from nearby buildings, window orientation, window size, number of light entry points, interior wall material, and brightness of interior wall-finishes.

mechanisms: Light is a fundamental element of our visual perception of interior space in the daytime, and thus is a central candidate for affecting the emotional state at home.

Daylight influences the circadian rhythm in both physiological behaviour – such as hormone secretion (cortisol and melatonin) – and body behaviour – such as lethargy, eating and sleeping – over a 24-h period.

Our visual perception of the built environment is constructed through the interaction of light sources with objects in the space, which have properties of reflection, absorption, refraction, scattering and diffraction.
The light stimuli that we process are perceived differently depending on their source, wavelength, exposure range and type of light.
Lighting conditions impact people's emotions at psychological and neurophysiological levels, triggering positive and negative experiences and expression of emotions.
implementation_implications: Natural Light Design (NLD) factors are fundamental for improving emotional subjective wellbeing (E-SWB) in the home.
Improvements to natural lighting in the home have a positive impact on E-SWB, particularly for women and younger populations.
The amount of daylight entering a house strongly impacts perceived happiness and sadness.
Rooms with windows facing the equator (sun-facing) lead to happier perceptions, regardless of cloudiness.
Window size is critical; windows covering >20% of the wall improve happiness and sadness, with >40% coverage yielding the largest E-SWB gains.
Perceived happiness and sadness improve when nearby buildings are >10m away from the dwelling.
Stucco and wood wall-finish surfaces are beneficial for perceived happiness, while brick surfaces are not.
Maximizing window size, despite potential energy/cost implications, is important for inhabitants' emotional wellbeing.
Housing policies and designs should prioritize windows oriented towards the equator to maximize emotional wellbeing.
Preserving and improving natural light conditions in housing should be a fundamental concern in built environment planning.

limitations: Results may not be generalizable to other population groups due to convenience sampling.
Results may not be generalizable to other geographical contexts as images were modeled for Santiago, Chile.
The study sample included a disproportionate number of young adults.
Photo-simulation technology relies on a person's capacity to imagine themselves in a 3D space from a single viewpoint, which may not capture the full indoor daylight experience.
Photo simulations are devoid of auditory stimuli, which could influence emotional responses.
Other environmental factors like smell or temperature were not included, which could influence perceptions.
